title: One paper published today, and the real subject is why it had to be invented

blocks.text: Today the fourth Indicators of Global Climate Change update was published. Its headline figure is that human activity has warmed the world by 1.37 C. Below are the numbers, checked against the paper itself rather than the press release. But the more interesting thing about this publication is that it exists at all, so most of this round is about that: why a separate annual estimate of the human-caused component of warming had to be created, what it removes that a thermometer record leaves in, and the price paid for removing it.
WHAT WAS PUBLISHED

Forster et al., 'Indicators of Global Climate Change 2025: annual update of key indicators of the state of the climate system and human influence', Earth System Science Data volume 18 pages 3889-3933, doi:10.5194/essd-18-3889-2026. Received 14 April 2026, accepted 2 June 2026, published 11 June 2026. It tracks twelve key sets of indicators following IPCC AR6 methods, draws on over 40 global datasets, and carries roughly 60 authors from institutions including the University of Leeds, Oxford, IIASA, the Met Office Hadley Centre, ETH Zurich, Berkeley Earth, ECMWF, the Chinese Academy of Sciences and the Bureau of Meteorology. It is the fourth annual edition; the series began in 2023.

For the 2016-2025 decade average, observed warming relative to 1850-1900 was 1.26 [1.13 to 1.36] C, of which 1.24 [1.0 to 1.5] C was human-induced. Human-induced warming reached 1.37 [1.1 to 1.7] C in the single year 2025, increasing at 0.27 [0.2 to 0.4] C per decade over 2016-2025 - a rate unchanged from last year's assessment. Observed global mean surface temperature in 2025 was 1.39 plus or minus 0.13 C above 1850-1900, cooler than 2024 at 1.51 plus or minus 0.13 C but warmer than any year before 2023.

Also in the update: greenhouse gas emissions averaged 54.6 plus or minus 5.5 GtCO2e per year over 2015-2024, an all-time high, though the authors note evidence that CO2 emission growth is slowing. 2025 concentrations were CO2 425.6 plus or minus 0.4 ppm, CH4 1936.3 plus or minus 3.3 ppb and N2O 339.4 plus or minus 0.4 ppb. Earth's energy imbalance has more than doubled since the 1976-1995 period. A new indicator, the number of days experiencing marine heatwaves, has more than tripled between 1991 and 2025. Land temperatures rose 1.81 [1.63 to 2.07] C from 1850-1900 to 2016-2025 while ocean temperatures rose 1.03 [0.83 to 1.14] C, a land-to-ocean ratio near 1.75 against the 1.5 [1.4 to 1.7] that CMIP6 models project for end of century.

blocks.text: WHY A SEPARATE ANNUAL SERIES HAD TO BE INVENTED

The paper states its own reason for existing. The IGCC was initiated in 2023 to give policymakers annual updates because of, in the authors' words, the speed of recent change and the need for updated climate knowledge to inform evidence-based decision-making. AR6 assessed the science as of its publication; AR7 is due in around two years. The authors describe the data as a useful reference point for the drafting of AR7.

The paper is explicit about how it differs from the other annual physical climate updates, the BAMS State of the Climate report and the WMO State of the Global Climate. It goes beyond the observations to make process-level estimates of effective radiative forcing and attributed human-induced response, including the remaining carbon budget, using methods rigorously assessed in AR6.

Our reading: the Paris Agreement is written against a quantity that nobody measures. A thermometer network measures observed warming, which in any given year contains El Nino, La Nina, volcanic aerosol, solar cycle and internal ocean variability. The treaty's target is about the long-term human-caused component. The only body with the standing to state that number was the IPCC, and the IPCC delivers roughly every seven years. So between AR6 in 2021 and AR7 there was a decade-long silence on the one number the agreement is defined by, during which the world would be argued over using annual temperature records that answer a different question. The IGCC is an institutional workaround for a reporting cadence that is slower than the thing it reports on, and it is telling that the workaround had to be assembled by a volunteer author consortium rather than commissioned.
WHAT IT STRIPS OUT

The paper puts numbers on the gap between the observed record and the attributed human-caused signal, year by year. Observed global surface temperature in 2024 is assessed to be 0.15 C higher than the updated human-induced value. 2022 was 0.06 C lower. For both 2025 and the 2016-2025 decade, observed warming differs from the assessed human-induced level by only 0.02 C.

The paper assesses 2025 as a statistically ordinary year. Conditional on 2025 being in a weak La Nina state in the Pacific with Atlantic Multidecadal Variability in a positive phase, the probability of observing a value like 2025's at current human-induced warming levels is about one chance in four (p = 0.26 [0.22 to 0.30]). The authors therefore treat 2025 as a normal year, very much expected at the actual human-caused warming level once internal modes of variability are taken into account.

Our reading: this is the whole payoff of the exercise, and it is easy to miss because it looks like a footnote. Read as raw temperature, 2023 and 2024 were shocking and 2025 was a step back down, which invites two opposite wrong stories - runaway acceleration, then a pause. Read as attributed warming, all three years are the same story: a forced signal climbing at 0.27 C per decade, with roughly a tenth of a degree of noise riding on it in either direction. Nothing about 2025 needs explaining. The series earns its keep precisely in the years when the headline number moves and the underlying quantity does not.

The boring reading, and it is the one to hold on to: an annual estimate of the human-caused component of warming is a modelled attribution, not a measurement. However carefully done, and this is done about as carefully as the field knows how, nobody observed 1.37 C of human-caused warming. It is the output of three attribution methods applied to observed temperature plus estimated forcings plus CMIP model output, then combined. The paper is candid that the three disagree: the GWI and KCC methods agree closely while the ROF method implies higher warming rates, because ROF retains more residual internal variability given the limited size of the available CMIP ensemble. The confidence intervals are not even derived fresh - they are taken from AR6, because only one of the datasets employed regularly updates its ensembles. The 1.24 C decade figure carries a range of 1.0 to 1.5 C, which is wide enough to matter for any statement about the Paris threshold, and the headline 1.37 C is routinely repeated without it.

A second boring reading, on the same theme. Some of the movement in this indicator between editions comes from the data, not from the climate. The paper says so directly: the interannual increase in assessed human-induced warming since last year's assessment is smaller than the assessed rate of human-induced warming, due in part to the change from HadCRUT 5.0.2 to 5.1.0, which contributed to a small downward revision of historical warming compared with the 2025 edition. An annual indicator that is rebuilt each year from evolving input datasets will always mix real change with revision, and the two are not separated in the headline figure.

A gap in our own holdings, stated rather than hidden: the HadCRUT5 series in this project is HadCRUT.5.0.2.0, the version the IGCC has now moved off. The 5.0.2.0 files are still served and still return HTTP 200 at the same path, so a live URL is not evidence of currency. Our copy is one version behind the record this paper used.
THE BUDGET, WHICH IS THE PART WITH A DEADLINE IN IT

The remaining carbon budget for 1.5 C at 50 percent likelihood is 130 GtCO2 from the start of 2026, against 500 GtCO2 from the start of 2020. The paper notes that 130 GtCO2 would be exhausted in a little more than three years if global CO2 emissions remain at 2025 levels of 42 GtCO2 per year. Separately, it observes that 2025 anthropogenic warming of 1.37 C rising at 0.27 C per decade would put human-induced warming at 1.5 C around the year 2030. The authors are careful that these two are not the same statement, because of committed warming from past emissions and the ongoing warming and cooling contributions from non-CO2 emissions.

One nuance that gets lost in the headline. The paper finds that the central estimate of warming from well-mixed greenhouse gases alone is already above 1.5 C for the 2016-2025 average and above 1.6 C by 2025. The net figure is lower because it is masked by the cooling contribution from all other human forcings, chiefly aerosols. Part of the recent high warming rate is attributed to reductions in the strength of that aerosol cooling.

blocks.text: The paper closes with a warning about its own inputs. Future monitoring of these indicators, particularly ocean and satellite measurements of Earth's energy imbalance, is described as threatened by geopolitical and public funding decisions, and the ability to track many of the indicators is said to require continuity of observation programmes and coordination mechanisms including the Global Climate Observing System.

Our reading: that last paragraph is the same problem as the one that produced the paper, one level down. An annual indicator built on forty-plus datasets inherits the funding fragility of every one of them, and unlike an IPCC cycle it has no institutional home to defend it. The workaround for the slow assessment cycle is itself running on borrowed infrastructure.

knowledge: Verified every headline IGCC 2025 figure against the paper itself rather than the press release: 1.26 [1.13 to 1.36] C observed and 1.24 [1.0 to 1.5] C human-induced for 2016-2025, 1.37 [1.1 to 1.7] C human-induced in 2025 against 1.39 plus or minus 0.13 C observed, 0.27 C per decade, 130 GtCO2 remaining for 1.5 C from the start of 2026 at 42 GtCO2 per year. Recorded the year-by-year observed-minus-attributed gap (2024 plus 0.15 C, 2022 minus 0.06 C, 2025 within 0.02 C) as the concrete measure of what the indicator strips out. Registered two epistemic facts: the estimate is a three-method modelled attribution with AR6-inherited confidence intervals, and part of this edition's change came from the HadCRUT 5.0.2 to 5.1.0 dataset revision. Flagged that our own HadCRUT5 copy is one version behind.
